readerTitle: When a customer says 'We're also talking to your rival'
caseNote: 가상 사례 (운송 회사 두 곳, 병원 예약 소프트웨어) + 일반적 관찰 (구매 부서의 복수 견적 관행). 검증 가능한 실제 기업 사례가 없어 company_story 대신 two_businesses 형식을 사용함.
insight: '경쟁사도 보고 있다'는 위협이 아니라 정보다. 고객이 무엇을, 어떤 기준으로 비교하는지 물으면 판매자는 가격이 아닌 기준을 두고 경쟁할 수 있다.
misconception: 고객이 경쟁사를 언급하면 가격을 맞춰 주거나 경쟁사의 약점을 짚어야 이길 수 있다.

sources.text: 영업·구매 실무의 일반적 관찰 (많은 조직이 일정 금액 이상 구매 시 복수 견적을 요구함)
운송 회사, 병원 예약 소프트웨어 사례와 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: '많은 구매 부서가 복수 견적을 요구한다'는 일반적 관행으로 서술했으며 특정 비율이나 통계는 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전 표현이 과장되지 않았는지 확인하세요.
모든 기업명, 가격(10% 인하, 30% 저렴), 사례 결과는 가상입니다. 실제 기업이나 연구로 오해되지 않도록 해당 카드에 illustrative: true를 붙였습니다.

cards.title: Same email, two very different replies.
body: Two regional freight companies each get the same email from a factory they deliver for: "We're also getting a quote from another carrier."
One cuts its price 10% that afternoon. The other replies with a single question. A month later, only one of them still has its full margin.

image.label: Two trucks, two reply bubbles: a price tag and a question mark
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 같은 공장 앞에 트럭 두 대. 왼쪽 트럭 위 말풍선에는 아래로 향한 가격표 "-10%", 오른쪽 트럭 위 말풍선에는 물음표. 실제 운송사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your customer is talking to a rival carrier.
body: You run a trucking company. A parts manufacturer you've served for two years says a competitor is quoting on their routes.

options.text: Offer to match any lower price they get
options.feedback: You may keep the account, but you give away margin before knowing if price is even the issue. You also teach them that naming a rival lowers your price.

options.text: Mention the rival's reputation for late deliveries
options.feedback: It may be true, but attacking a rival often makes buyers defend the option they're considering. Better to let them discover gaps through their own criteria.

options.text: Ask what prompted the comparison and what matters most to them
options.feedback: You learn what you're actually competing on before you spend anything. It costs a day, and it may reveal the deal isn't about price at all.

cards.title: One seller guessed. The other asked.
body: The first carrier guessed the problem was price. It kept the contract at a thinner margin, and the factory now asks for a rival quote every year.
The second asked why they were looking. The answer: two late trucks last quarter had stopped a production line. The rival was cheaper, but the real worry was **missed delivery windows**.
So the carrier showed its on-time record and offered a credit for any late load. It kept the contract at the original price.

cards.title: The competitor objection is a request to compare.
body: When a customer says "We're looking at a competitor," they're telling you a choice is underway. That's **information**, not an attack.

Your job isn't to win an argument against the rival. It's to find out *what* is being compared, *on which criteria*, and *who* decides. Then you compete on the criteria that matter to the customer, not on the ones you fear.

image.label: A balance scale with labeled criteria on each side
image.brief: 저울 일러스트. 양쪽 접시에 "Price", "On-time delivery", "Support", "Switching effort" 라벨이 붙은 블록들. 고객의 손이 블록 하나를 고르는 장면. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: The same sentence can mean four things.
body: Each meaning calls for a different response. Asking is how you tell them apart.

breakdown.label: A rule
breakdown.detail: Many purchasing teams must collect more than one quote

breakdown.label: Leverage
breakdown.detail: They like you and want a better price

breakdown.label: A real gap
breakdown.detail: Something isn't working, like late trucks

breakdown.label: Reassurance
breakdown.detail: They want to feel the choice was checked

cards.title: Three questions to ask before you respond.
list: **What made you start looking?** This surfaces the real trigger.
**What would the right choice look like for you?** This sets the criteria.
**Who else weighs in on the decision?** A finance lead and a plant manager compare differently.
cards.callout: Answer the comparison they're making, not the one you imagine.

cards.title: Sometimes the rival really is the better fit.
body: If their criteria point to the competitor, say so. You lose one deal, but you gain trust, and customers who leave on good terms often come back or refer others.
Also know when you're only a price check. If a buyer won't share criteria and just wants your number, give it plainly. Don't pour weeks into a deal that was decided before you arrived.

cards.title: Now it's software for clinics.
body: You sell appointment-booking software. A dental clinic says: "Another tool has the same features and costs 30% less."

options.text: Send a 40-row feature table showing you win on most rows
options.feedback: It shows effort, but it compares on your terms. The clinic may only care about three of those rows.

options.text: Ask which tasks they need on day one and what switching would involve, then offer a trial with their own schedule
options.feedback: You shift the comparison to what the clinic will actually use and how hard it is to move. You spend time setting up a trial, but you learn whether you truly fit.

options.text: Cut your price 30% to close it this week
options.feedback: You remove one difference and keep the deal, but every future renewal starts from the lower number. And you never learned what they valued.

cards.softwareNote: In software, switching effort, like moving data and retraining staff, is often a bigger part of the real comparison than the monthly price.

cards.title: When a rival comes up, ask before you answer.
body: "We're looking at a competitor" tells you a comparison is happening. Find out what's being compared and why, then compete on the criteria that matter to the customer.
**Try it today:** think of the last deal where a rival came up. Write down what the customer was really comparing. Did you know at the time?
